meta.title: Vietnamese B2 Upper Intermediate
meta.subtitle: 1500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Vietnamese → English (see the Vietnamese, recall the meaning) and English → Vietnamese (see an English meaning, recall the Vietnamese). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1500 words for an upper-intermediate learner, aligned to B2 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand the main ideas of complex text on both concrete and abstract topics, including technical discussions in their field of specialisation' — a learner here is able to interact with a degree of fluency and spontaneity that makes regular interaction with native speakers quite possible without strain for either party, and to produce clear, detailed text on a wide range of subjects and explain a viewpoint on a topical issue, giving the advantages and disadvantages of various options. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: Vietnam's own framework for learners of Vietnamese publishes no graded word list, and neither does any exam board, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 166 of the 1500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — politics and public administration, the law and the courts, the economy and finance, science and research, technology, the environment and natural resources, health and the mind, the arts, literature and the media, history and society, argument and evaluation — the words for claims, evidence, causes and consequences — the formal connectors of written Vietnamese, and the verbs of reporting, analysing and persuading — and the other 1334 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Vietnamese, counted in film and television subtitles. Vietnamese writes a space between syllables rather than between words, so the subtitles were divided into words against the dictionary first, and a two-syllable word such as học sinh (pupil) is counted as one word. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Beneath every headword its tones are named, one per syllable — ngang (no mark), huyền (à), sắc (á), hỏi (ả), ngã (ã) and nặng (ạ) — read off the marks the word is spelt with. 131 nouns show their classifier, the word that stands between a number and the noun (hai con mèo, two cats), and 637 words borrowed from Chinese show the characters they come from. The pronunciation is given in IPA for Hanoi and, where it differs, for Saigon. Real example sentences come with 1133 of the 1500 words, three apiece for 692 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Spellings are Wiktionary's, which often puts the tone mark in the older place (hoà, khoẻ); the newer (hòa, khỏe) is equally correct. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, classifiers, characters and pronunciation: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: the OpenSubtitles 2018 Vietnamese text (opensubtitles.org, via the OPUS corpus collection), counted here. Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
